questions.q: Find the wave number of the $4^{\text{th}}$ line in the Lyman series of H spectrum. (R $=$ Rydberg constant)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The bond enthalpies of H-H, Cl-Cl, and H-Cl bonds are 437 kJ/mol, 239 kJ/mol, and 433 kJ/mol respectively. Calculate the enthalpy of formation of HCl.
questions.solution:
The reaction for the formation of HCl is:

$\dfrac{1}{2} \text{H}_2(g) + \dfrac{1}{2} \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{HCl}(g)$

The enthalpy of formation $\Delta H_f$ is given by the difference between the bond enthalpies of reactants and products:

$\Delta H_f = \sum \text{BE}(\text{reactants}) - \sum \text{BE}(\text{products})$

$\Delta H_f = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \text{BE}(\text{H-H}) + \dfrac{1}{2} \text{BE}(\text{Cl-Cl}) \right) - \text{BE}(\text{H-Cl})$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta H_f = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \times 437 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 239 \right) - 433$

$\Delta H_f = (218.5 + 119.5) - 433$

$\Delta H_f = 338 - 433 = -95 \text{ kJ/mol}$

Answer: $-95$ kJ/mol

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following is applicable for isothermal process?
questions.solution:
For an isothermal process, the temperature of the system remains constant, which means $\Delta T = 0$.

For an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is given by $\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$. Since $\Delta T = 0$, the change in internal energy is zero, so $\Delta U = 0$.

According to the first law of thermodynamics:
$\Delta U = Q + W$

Substituting $\Delta U = 0$ into the equation, we get:
$0 = Q + W$

$W = -Q$

This indicates that the work done on the system is equal to the negative of the heat absorbed by the system.

Answer: $W=-Q$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the work done in the formation of 1 mole gaseous methane from solid carbon and gaseous hydrogen at $27^\circ\text{C}$? ($R=8.314\ \text{J k}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the formation of $1$ mole of gaseous methane is:

$\text{C(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_4\text{(g)}$

The change in the number of moles of gaseous substances ($\Delta n_g$) is:

$\Delta n_g = n_{g,\text{products}} - n_{g,\text{reactants}}$

$\Delta n_g = 1 - 2 = -1$

The work done ($W$) during a chemical reaction at constant temperature and pressure is given by:

$W = -\Delta n_g R T$

Given:
$R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$
$T = 27^\circ\text{C} = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$

Substituting the values:

$W = -(-1) \times 8.314 \times 300$

$W = +2494.2 \text{ J}$

$W = +2.4942 \text{ kJ}$

Answer: $+2.4942$ kJ

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A series LCR circuit is connected across a source E of e.m.f. $E=15\sin\left(50\pi t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$. The current from the supply is $I=5\sin\left(50\pi t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$. The impedance of the circuit and the phase difference between e.m.f. and current are, respectively, [all the quantities in the above two equations are in SI units.]
questions.solution:
Given the equations for e.m.f. and current:

$E = 15\sin\left(50\pi t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

$I = 5\sin\left(50\pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$

The peak voltage is $E_0 = 15$ V and the peak current is $I_0 = 5$ A.

The impedance of the circuit is given by:

$Z = \dfrac{E_0}{I_0} = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3\ \Omega$

The phase of the e.m.f. is $\phi_E = 50\pi t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and the phase of the current is $\phi_I = 50\pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

The phase difference $\Delta \phi$ between the e.m.f. and the current is:

$\Delta \phi = |\phi_I - \phi_E| = \left|\left(50\pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - \left(50\pi t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right|$

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{3\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

Thus, the impedance is $3\ \Omega$ and the phase difference is $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^{c}$.

Answer: $3\ \Omega,\ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^{c}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The alternating voltage is given by $V=V_0\sin\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$. When will the voltage be maximum for the first time?
$\{\sin(90)^\circ=1\}$
questions.solution:
The given alternating voltage is $V = V_0 \sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

For the voltage to be maximum, the value of the sine function must be $1$.

$\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 1$

The first maximum occurs when the phase angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

Substituting $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$:

$\dfrac{2\pi}{T} t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

$t = \dfrac{T}{6}$

Answer: $\dfrac{T}{6}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An alternating voltage is given as, $E=100\sqrt{2}\sin 100t$
This voltage E is applied to a capacitor of $1\ \mu\text{F}$. The current reading in an a.c. ammeter in mA is
questions.solution:
Given alternating voltage is $E = 100\sqrt{2}\sin(100t)$

Comparing with the standard equation $E = E_0\sin(\omega t)$, we get:

Peak voltage, $E_0 = 100\sqrt{2}$ V

Angular frequency, $\omega = 100$ rad/s

The rms voltage is $E_{rms} = \dfrac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 100$ V

Capacitive reactance, $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{100 \times 10^{-6}} = 10^4\ \Omega$

The reading of an a.c. ammeter is the rms current, which is given by:

$I_{rms} = \dfrac{E_{rms}}{X_C} = \dfrac{100}{10^4} = 10^{-2}$ A

Converting to milliamperes:

$I_{rms} = 10^{-2} \times 1000$ mA $= 10$ mA

Answer: $10$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three identical parallel plate air capacitors are connected in series to a battery of e.m.f. V. If two capacitors are completely filled with dielectric material of constant k, then potential difference across the third capacitor will become
questions.solution:
Let the capacitance of each identical air capacitor be $C$.

When two capacitors are completely filled with a dielectric material of constant $k$, their capacitances become $kC$ and $kC$. The third capacitor remains an air capacitor with capacitance $C$.

The equivalent capacitance $C_{eq}$ of the three capacitors connected in series is given by:

$\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{kC} + \dfrac{1}{kC} + \dfrac{1}{C}$

$\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}} = \dfrac{2}{kC} + \dfrac{k}{kC} = \dfrac{k+2}{kC}$

$C_{eq} = \dfrac{kC}{k+2}$

The total charge $Q$ drawn from the battery of e.m.f. $V$ is:

$Q = C_{eq}V = \dfrac{kCV}{k+2}$

In a series circuit, the charge on each capacitor is the same. Therefore, the potential difference $V_3$ across the third capacitor (capacitance $C$) is:

$V_3 = \dfrac{Q}{C} = \dfrac{\dfrac{kCV}{k+2}}{C} = \dfrac{kV}{k+2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{kV}{(k+2)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The amount of work done in increasing voltage across the plates of capacitor from 5 V to 10 V is W. The work done in increasing it from 10 V to 20 V is
questions.solution:
The work done in increasing the voltage across a capacitor is equal to the change in its electrostatic potential energy.

$W = \Delta U = \dfrac{1}{2} C (V_f^2 - V_i^2)$

For the first case, the voltage increases from $5$ V to $10$ V:

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} C (10^2 - 5^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} C (100 - 25) = \dfrac{75}{2} C$

For the second case, the voltage increases from $10$ V to $20$ V:

$W' = \dfrac{1}{2} C (20^2 - 10^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} C (400 - 100) = \dfrac{300}{2} C$

Taking the ratio of the two work done values:

$\dfrac{W'}{W} = \dfrac{300}{75} = 4$

$W' = 4W$

Answer: $4W$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A resistance is to be measured using a meter bridge; the student chooses the standard resistance R to be $100\ \Omega$. The student finds the null point at $l_1=16$ cm. To get the null point near the middle of the wire, the value of R will be
questions.solution:
For a meter bridge, the balance condition is given by $\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$, where $X$ is the unknown resistance and $R$ is the standard resistance.

Given $R = 100\ \Omega$ and $l = 16$ cm, we can find $X$:

$\dfrac{X}{100} = \dfrac{16}{100 - 16} = \dfrac{16}{84}$

$X = \dfrac{1600}{84} = \dfrac{400}{21} \approx 19.04\ \Omega$

To obtain the null point near the middle of the wire, the balancing length should be $l' \approx 50$ cm. Using the balance condition again with the new standard resistance $R'$:

$\dfrac{X}{R'} = \dfrac{50}{100 - 50} = 1$

$R' = X \approx 19.04\ \Omega$

Thus, the value of the standard resistance should be chosen as $19\ \Omega$.

Answer: $19\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A potentiometer wire has length 4 m and resistance $8\ \Omega$. The resistance that must be connected in series with the wire and the driving battery of e.m.f. 2 V, so as to get a potential gradient of 1 mV per cm on the wire is
questions.solution:
Potential gradient $k = 1\text{ mV/cm} = \dfrac{10^{-3}\text{ V}}{10^{-2}\text{ m}} = 0.1\text{ V/m}$

Length of the potentiometer wire $L = 4\text{ m}$

Potential difference across the potentiometer wire $V = k \times L = 0.1 \times 4 = 0.4\text{ V}$

Current in the circuit $I = \dfrac{V}{R_p} = \dfrac{0.4}{8} = 0.05\text{ A}$

Total resistance of the circuit $R_{eq} = \dfrac{E}{I} = \dfrac{2}{0.05} = 40\ \Omega$

Resistance to be connected in series $R = R_{eq} - R_p = 40 - 8 = 32\ \Omega$

Answer: $32\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a photoelectric cell, for the incident radiation of wavelength $\lambda$, the fastest electron has speed 'v'. If the wavelength of incident radiation is changed to $\dfrac{\lambda}{3}$, the speed of the fastest emitted electron is
questions.solution:
Using Einstein's photoelectric equation:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi$

When the wavelength is changed to $\dfrac{\lambda}{3}$, the new maximum kinetic energy is:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv'^2 = \dfrac{3hc}{\lambda} - \phi$

Substituting $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \phi$ into the second equation:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv'^2 = 3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \phi\right) - \phi$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv'^2 = 3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\right) + 2\phi$

Since the work function $\phi \gt 0$, we get:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv'^2 \gt 3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\right)$

$v'^2 \gt 3v^2$

$v' \gt v\sqrt{3}$

Thus, the speed of the fastest emitted electron is greater than $v(\sqrt{3})$.

Answer: greater than $v(\sqrt{3})$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The additional energy that should be given to an electron to reduce its de-Broglie wavelength from 1 nm to 0.5 nm is $x$ times the initial kinetic energy. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
The de-Broglie wavelength of an electron is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$

Squaring both sides, we get $K = \dfrac{h^2}{2m\lambda^2}$

This implies $K \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}$

For the initial state, $\lambda_1 = 1$ nm, so $K_1 \propto \dfrac{1}{1^2} = 1$

For the final state, $\lambda_2 = 0.5$ nm, so $K_2 \propto \dfrac{1}{(0.5)^2} = 4$

Therefore, $K_2 = 4K_1$

The additional energy required is $\Delta K = K_2 - K_1 = 4K_1 - K_1 = 3K_1$

Given that the additional energy is $x$ times the initial kinetic energy, we have $x = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Semicircular wire of radius R is rotated in a uniform magnetic field about an axis passing through its ends. If the frequency of rotation is f, the amplitude of induced e.m.f. in the wire is [B$=$magnetic field induction]
questions.solution:
The area of the semicircular region is $A = \dfrac{1}{2} \pi R^2$.

We can consider a closed loop formed by the semicircular wire and the straight segment joining its ends. Since this straight segment lies on the axis of rotation, its velocity is zero, and no motional emf is induced in it. Therefore, the emf induced in the semicircular wire is equal to the emf induced in the entire closed loop.

Assuming the magnetic field is perpendicular to the axis of rotation for maximum induced emf, the magnetic flux through the loop at any instant $t$ is given by $\Phi = B A \cos(\omega t)$, where $\omega = 2 \pi f$ is the angular frequency of rotation.

According to Faraday's law of induction, the induced emf is $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = B A \omega \sin(\omega t)$.

The amplitude of the induced emf is $\varepsilon_{0} = B A \omega$.

Substituting $A = \dfrac{1}{2} \pi R^2$ and $\omega = 2 \pi f$, we get:

$\varepsilon_{0} = B \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \pi R^2\right) (2 \pi f) = \pi^2 R^2 f B$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $l$ in the form of a square loop is in a plane normal to magnetic field B. If the length of the wire is decreasing at the rate $\dfrac{dl}{dt}$, the e.m.f. induced is $e_1$. If this wire is converted into a circular loop, the e.m.f. induced in a circular loop is $e_2$. Then $\dfrac{e_1}{e_2}$ is
questions.solution:
For the square loop, the side length is $a = \dfrac{l}{4}$.

Area of the square loop is $A_1 = a^2 = \dfrac{l^2}{16}$.

The induced e.m.f. $e_1$ is given by $e_1 = \left| \dfrac{d\Phi_1}{dt} \right| = B \dfrac{dA_1}{dt} = B \dfrac{d}{dt} \left( \dfrac{l^2}{16} \right) = \dfrac{Bl}{8} \left| \dfrac{dl}{dt} \right|$.

For the circular loop, the circumference is $l$, so the radius is $r = \dfrac{l}{2\pi}$.

Area of the circular loop is $A_2 = \pi r^2 = \pi \left( \dfrac{l}{2\pi} \right)^2 = \dfrac{l^2}{4\pi}$.

The induced e.m.f. $e_2$ is given by $e_2 = \left| \dfrac{d\Phi_2}{dt} \right| = B \dfrac{dA_2}{dt} = B \dfrac{d}{dt} \left( \dfrac{l^2}{4\pi} \right) = \dfrac{Bl}{2\pi} \left| \dfrac{dl}{dt} \right|$.

Taking the ratio of the two induced e.m.f.s:

$\dfrac{e_1}{e_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{Bl}{8} \left| \dfrac{dl}{dt} \right|}{\dfrac{Bl}{2\pi} \left| \dfrac{dl}{dt} \right|} = \dfrac{2\pi}{8} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A thin semicircular conducting ring (PQR) of radius r is falling with its plane vertical in a horizontal magnetic field B as shown in the figure. The potential difference developed across the ring when its speed is v, is
$\{\sin(90)^\circ=1\}$
options: $\pi rBv$ and terminal R is at higher potential
$\dfrac{Bv\pi r^{2}}{2}$ and terminal P is at higher potential
$2rBv$ and terminal R is at higher potential
questions.solution:
The motional emf induced in a conductor moving in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\varepsilon = (\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{l}$, where $\vec{l}$ is the vector connecting the ends of the conductor.

For the semicircular ring PQR, the effective length vector $\vec{l}$ is the straight line from P to R, which has a magnitude equal to the diameter of the semicircle.

$l_{\text{eff}} = 2r$

Since $\vec{v}$, $\vec{B}$, and $\vec{l}$ are mutually perpendicular, the magnitude of the induced motional emf is:

$\varepsilon = B v l_{\text{eff}} = 2rBv$

The polarity of the induced emf is determined by the direction of the magnetic force on the positive charges, given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

The velocity $\vec{v}$ is directed downwards and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is directed into the plane of the paper.

By the right-hand rule, the cross product $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$ points towards the right.

This means positive charges are pushed towards terminal R, making it at a higher potential than terminal P.

Therefore, the potential difference developed across the ring is $2rBv$ with terminal R at a higher potential.

Answer: $2rBv$ and terminal R is at higher potential

questions.q: Three charges Q, $+q$ and $+q$ are placed at the vertices of the right angle triangle (isosceles triangle) as shown. The net electrostatic energy of the configuration is zero, if Q is equal to [a $=$ length of two equal sides of a triangle]
questions.solution:
The net electrostatic potential energy of a system of charges is the sum of the potential energies of all pairs of charges.

Let the charges be placed at the vertices of the right-angled isosceles triangle. From the given figure, the charges are $Q$, $+q$, and $+q$.
The distances between the pairs of charges are:
1. Distance between $Q$ and $+q$ (vertical side) $= a$
2. Distance between $+q$ and $+q$ (horizontal side) $= a$
3. Distance between $Q$ and $+q$ (hypotenuse) $= \sqrt{a^2 + a^2} = a\sqrt{2}$

The total electrostatic potential energy $U$ of the system is given by:
$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{Q \cdot q}{a} + \dfrac{q \cdot q}{a} + \dfrac{Q \cdot q}{a\sqrt{2}} \right)$

Given that the net electrostatic energy of the configuration is zero, we have $U = 0$:
$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{Qq}{a} + \dfrac{q^2}{a} + \dfrac{Qq}{a\sqrt{2}} \right) = 0$

Dividing the entire equation by $\dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 a}$ (assuming $q \neq 0$), we get:
$Q + q + \dfrac{Q}{\sqrt{2}} = 0$

Grouping the terms with $Q$:
$Q \left( 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) + q = 0$

$Q \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{2} + 1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = -q$

$Q = \dfrac{-\sqrt{2}q}{\sqrt{2} + 1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{-\sqrt{2}q}{1+\sqrt{2}}$

questions.q: Three metallic spherical shells (not concentric) of radii R, 2R and 4R are given charges $Q_1$, $Q_2$ and $Q_3$ respectively. It is found that the surface charge densities on the outer surfaces of the shells are equal. Then, the ratio of the charges $Q_1:Q_2:Q_3$, is
questions.solution:
For isolated (not concentric) metallic spherical shells, the charge given to each shell resides entirely on its outer surface.

The surface charge density $\sigma$ of a spherical shell of radius $r$ and charge $Q$ is given by:
$\sigma = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi r^2}$

Given that the surface charge densities on the outer surfaces of the three shells are equal:
$\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma_3$

Substituting the values of charges and radii for each shell:
$\dfrac{Q_1}{4\pi R^2} = \dfrac{Q_2}{4\pi (2R)^2} = \dfrac{Q_3}{4\pi (4R)^2}$

$\dfrac{Q_1}{R^2} = \dfrac{Q_2}{4R^2} = \dfrac{Q_3}{16R^2}$

Multiplying by $R^2$, we get the ratio of the charges:
$Q_1 : Q_2 : Q_3 = 1 : 4 : 16$

Answer: $1:4:16$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: There are two vessels A and B with rigid walls containing ideal gases. The pressure, temperature and volume are $P_A$, $T_A$ and V in the vessel A and $P_B$, $T_B$ and V in vessel B. The vessels are now connected through a small tube. In equilibrium, pressure is P and temperature is T, then $\dfrac{P}{T}$ is {number of moles of gas in vessel A $=$ number of moles of gas in vessel B}
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation, the initial number of moles in vessel A is:

$n_A = \dfrac{P_A V}{R T_A}$

The initial number of moles in vessel B is:

$n_B = \dfrac{P_B V}{R T_B}$

When the vessels are connected, the total volume becomes $V_{total} = V + V = 2V$. Let the equilibrium pressure be $P$ and the equilibrium temperature be $T$. The total number of moles in the system remains conserved:

$n_{total} = n_A + n_B$

$\dfrac{P(2V)}{RT} = \dfrac{P_A V}{RT_A} + \dfrac{P_B V}{RT_B}$

Dividing the entire equation by $\dfrac{V}{R}$:

$\dfrac{2P}{T} = \dfrac{P_A}{T_A} + \dfrac{P_B}{T_B}$

$\dfrac{P}{T} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{P_A}{T_A} + \dfrac{P_B}{T_B}\right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{P_A}{T_A}+\dfrac{P_B}{T_B}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a cyclotron, for the same values of B and R, what is the ratio of the maximum kinetic energies of $\alpha$ particles and deuteron? {Mass of deuteron $=2m_p$, charge on deuteron $=+e$}
questions.solution:
The maximum kinetic energy of a particle in a cyclotron is given by $K = \dfrac{q^2 B^2 R^2}{2m}$.

For an $\alpha$ particle, charge $q_{\alpha} = 2e$ and mass $m_{\alpha} = 4m_p$.

$K_{\alpha} = \dfrac{(2e)^2 B^2 R^2}{2(4m_p)} = \dfrac{4e^2 B^2 R^2}{8m_p} = \dfrac{e^2 B^2 R^2}{2m_p}$

For a deuteron, charge $q_d = e$ and mass $m_d = 2m_p$.

$K_d = \dfrac{e^2 B^2 R^2}{2(2m_p)} = \dfrac{e^2 B^2 R^2}{4m_p}$

The ratio of their maximum kinetic energies is:

$\dfrac{K_{\alpha}}{K_d} = \dfrac{\dfrac{e^2 B^2 R^2}{2m_p}}{\dfrac{e^2 B^2 R^2}{4m_p}} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.q:
If the current 'i' is passing through the wire, it has a shape as shown in the figure. The radius of the curved part is R and the linear part is assumed to be very long. The magnetic induction of the field at the point O, is
($\mu_0=$permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
The wire can be divided into three parts: a lower semi-infinite straight wire, a semicircular arc, and an upper semi-infinite straight wire.

The magnetic field at point O due to the lower semi-infinite straight wire is given by $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}$. Applying the right-hand rule, the current is towards the left and point O is above the wire, so the magnetic field is directed into the page.

The magnetic field at point O due to the semicircular arc is given by $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4R} = \dfrac{\pi \mu_0 i}{4\pi R}$. The current is in the clockwise direction, so the magnetic field is directed into the page.

The magnetic field at point O due to the upper semi-infinite straight wire is given by $B_3 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}$. The current is towards the right and point O is below the wire, so the magnetic field is directed into the page.

Since all three magnetic field components are in the same direction, the total magnetic field at O is their sum:

$B_{net} = B_1 + B_2 + B_3$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R} + \dfrac{\pi \mu_0 i}{4\pi R} + \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}(1 + \pi + 1)$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}(2 + \pi)$

questions.q:
There are four lightweight rod samples P, Q, R and S separately suspended by thread. A bar magnet is slowly brought near to each sample and the following observations are noted
(a) P is weakly repelled
(b) R is strongly attracted
(c) S remains unaffected
(d) Q is weakly attracted
Which of the following is true?
options: R is of a diamagnetic material
P is of a non-magnetic material
S is of a ferromagnetic material
Q is of a paramagnetic material
questions.solution:
When a bar magnet is brought near a material, the magnetic behavior can be identified by the interaction:

Diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled by a magnetic field. Since P is weakly repelled, P is a diamagnetic material.

Ferromagnetic materials are strongly attracted by a magnetic field. Since R is strongly attracted, R is a ferromagnetic material.

Non-magnetic materials are unaffected by a magnetic field. Since S remains unaffected, S is a non-magnetic material.

Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted by a magnetic field. Since Q is weakly attracted, Q is a paramagnetic material.

Comparing these conclusions with the given options, the statement that Q is of a paramagnetic material is true.

Answer: Q is of a paramagnetic material

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The physical quantity $P=\dfrac{a^{3}b^{2}}{c^{1/3}d^{1/4}}$, where the percentage error in a, b, c, and d are $1\%$, $\dfrac{3}{2}\%$, $3\%$, and $2\%$ respectively. Then the percentage error in P is
questions.solution:
Given $P = \dfrac{a^{3}b^{2}}{c^{1/3}d^{1/4}}$

The maximum percentage error in $P$ is given by:

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100 = 3 \left(\dfrac{\Delta a}{a} \times 100\right) + 2 \left(\dfrac{\Delta b}{b} \times 100\right) + \dfrac{1}{3} \left(\dfrac{\Delta c}{c} \times 100\right) + \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{\Delta d}{d} \times 100\right)$

Substituting the given percentage errors:

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100 = 3(1\%) + 2\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\%\right) + \dfrac{1}{3}(3\%) + \dfrac{1}{4}(2\%)$

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100 = 3\% + 3\% + 1\% + 0.5\% = 7.5\%$

Answer: $7.5\ \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are expressed as $\vec{A}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}$. Unit vector perpendicular to $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is
questions.solution:
Given vectors are $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}$.

A vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is given by their cross product $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$.

$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = (2\hat{i} + \hat{j}) \times (\hat{i} - \hat{j})$

$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 2(\hat{i} \times \hat{i}) - 2(\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) + (\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) - (\hat{j} \times \hat{j})$

Since $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{j} = 0$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, and $\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}$:

$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0 - 2\hat{k} - \hat{k} - 0 = -3\hat{k}$

The magnitude of this vector is $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = |-3\hat{k}| = 3$.

The unit vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is:

$\hat{n} = \dfrac{\vec{A} \times \vec{B}}{|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|} = \dfrac{-3\hat{k}}{3} = -\hat{k}$

Answer: $-\hat{k}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For uniform acceleration in linear motion which of the following is NOT CORRECT?
options: The area under the velocity-time graph equals the displacement.
Acceleration is the slope of velocity-time graph.
questions.solution:
For uniform acceleration in linear motion, the acceleration $a$ is constant.

The kinematic equation for velocity is $v = u + at$, which represents a linear relationship between velocity $v$ and time $t$.

Thus, the velocity-time graph is a straight line (linear).

The slope of the velocity-time graph gives the acceleration, and the area under it gives the displacement.

Therefore, the statement 'Velocity-time graph is non-linear' is incorrect.

Answer: Velocity-time graph is non-linear.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spherical nuclei have mass numbers 216 and 64 with their radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ respectively. The ratio $\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}$ is
questions.solution:
The radius of a nucleus is related to its mass number $A$ by the empirical formula:

$R = R_0 A^{1/3}$

For the first nucleus with mass number $A_1 = 216$:

$R_1 = R_0 (216)^{1/3} = 6 R_0$

For the second nucleus with mass number $A_2 = 64$:

$R_2 = R_0 (64)^{1/3} = 4 R_0$

The ratio of their radii is:

$\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{6 R_0}{4 R_0} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Thus, the ratio is $3:2$.

Answer: $3:2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioactive nucleus ${}_{92}X^{235}$ decays to ${}_{91}Y^{231}$. Which of the following particles are emitted?
options: One alpha and one beta particle
questions.solution:
The decay reaction can be written as:

${}_{92}X^{235} \rightarrow {}_{91}Y^{231} + n_{\alpha} ({}_{2}He^{4}) + n_{\beta} ({}_{-1}e^{0})$

By conservation of mass number:

$235 = 231 + 4n_{\alpha} + 0$

$4n_{\alpha} = 4 \Rightarrow n_{\alpha} = 1$

By conservation of atomic number:

$92 = 91 + 2n_{\alpha} - n_{\beta}$

$92 = 91 + 2(1) - n_{\beta}$

$92 = 93 - n_{\beta} \Rightarrow n_{\beta} = 1$

Thus, one alpha particle and one beta particle are emitted.

Answer: One alpha and one beta particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles A and B execute S.H.M.s of periods T and $\dfrac{5T}{2}$. If they start from the mean position, then the phase difference between them when the particle A completes two oscillations will be (in radian)
questions.solution:
Time taken by particle A to complete two oscillations is $t = 2T$.

The phase of a particle executing S.H.M. starting from the mean position at time $t$ is given by $\phi = \omega t = \dfrac{2\pi}{T'}t$, where $T'$ is the time period.

For particle A, the phase at $t = 2T$ is:
$\phi_A = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} \times 2T = 4\pi$

For particle B, the time period is $T_B = \dfrac{5T}{2}$. The phase at $t = 2T$ is:
$\phi_B = \dfrac{2\pi}{\dfrac{5T}{2}} \times 2T = \dfrac{4\pi}{5T} \times 2T = \dfrac{8\pi}{5}$

The phase difference between the two particles is:
$\Delta\phi = \phi_A - \phi_B = 4\pi - \dfrac{8\pi}{5} = \dfrac{12\pi}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{12\pi}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is suspended from the two light springs separately. The periods of vertical oscillations are T and 3T respectively. The same body is suspended from two springs connected first in parallel and then in series. The periods of oscillation in both cases, respectively, are
questions.solution:
The time period of a spring-mass system is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$, which implies $k = \dfrac{4\pi^2 m}{T^2}$.

For the first spring:
$k_1 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 m}{T^2}$

For the second spring:
$k_2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 m}{(3T)^2} = \dfrac{4\pi^2 m}{9T^2}$

When the springs are connected in parallel, the equivalent spring constant is $k_p = k_1 + k_2$.
$\dfrac{1}{T_p^2} = \dfrac{k_p}{4\pi^2 m} = \dfrac{k_1 + k_2}{4\pi^2 m} = \dfrac{1}{T_1^2} + \dfrac{1}{T_2^2}$
$\dfrac{1}{T_p^2} = \dfrac{1}{T^2} + \dfrac{1}{9T^2} = \dfrac{10}{9T^2}$
$T_p = \dfrac{3T}{\sqrt{10}}$

When the springs are connected in series, the equivalent spring constant is given by $\dfrac{1}{k_s} = \dfrac{1}{k_1} + \dfrac{1}{k_2}$.
$T_s^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 m}{k_s} = 4\pi^2 m \left(\dfrac{1}{k_1} + \dfrac{1}{k_2}\right) = T_1^2 + T_2^2$
$T_s^2 = T^2 + (3T)^2 = 10T^2$
$T_s = \sqrt{10}T$

The periods of oscillation in parallel and series are $\dfrac{3T}{\sqrt{10}}$ and $\sqrt{10}T$ respectively.

Answer: $\dfrac{3T}{\sqrt{10}},\ \sqrt{10}T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the length of seconds pendulum on the surface of the earth is 1 m. The length of the seconds pendulum on the surface of the planet is $\left\{g_{planet}=\dfrac{7}{2}g_{earth}\right\}$ {periodic time of the seconds pendulum is same on both planets}
questions.solution:
The time period of a simple pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$.

Since the time period of a seconds pendulum is constant ($T = 2\ s$), we have $\dfrac{l}{g} = \text{constant}$.

$\dfrac{l_{earth}}{g_{earth}} = \dfrac{l_{planet}}{g_{planet}}$

Substituting the given values $l_{earth} = 1\ m$ and $g_{planet} = \dfrac{7}{2}g_{earth}$:

$\dfrac{1}{g_{earth}} = \dfrac{l_{planet}}{\dfrac{7}{2}g_{earth}}$

$l_{planet} = \dfrac{7}{2}\ m$

Answer: $\dfrac{7}{2}\ m$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ray of light passes through four transparent media with refractive indices $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$, $\mu_3$ and $\mu_4$ as shown in the figure. The surfaces of all media are parallel. If the emergent ray CD is parallel to the incident ray AB, then
questions.solution:
Let $\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3$, and $\theta_4$ be the angles made by the light ray with the normal in the media with refractive indices $\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3$, and $\mu_4$ respectively.

Applying Snell's law at each parallel interface, we get:

$\mu_1 \sin \theta_1 = \mu_2 \sin \theta_2 = \mu_3 \sin \theta_3 = \mu_4 \sin \theta_4$

It is given that the incident ray AB in the first medium is parallel to the emergent ray CD in the fourth medium. This means the angle of the ray with the normal in the first medium is equal to the angle of the ray with the normal in the fourth medium.

Therefore, $\theta_1 = \theta_4$.

From the Snell's law equation, we have:

$\mu_1 \sin \theta_1 = \mu_4 \sin \theta_4$

Substituting $\theta_1 = \theta_4$, we get:

$\mu_1 \sin \theta_1 = \mu_4 \sin \theta_1$

$\Rightarrow \mu_1 = \mu_4$

Answer: $\mu_4=\mu_1$

questions.q: An object is placed 15 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm, then the nature of the image formed will be
questions.solution:
Given object distance $u = -15$ cm and focal length $f = -10$ cm.

Using the mirror formula:

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{2 - 3}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$

$v = -30$ cm

Magnification $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-30}{-15} = -2$

Since $m$ is negative, the image is real and inverted. Since $|m| \gt 1$, the image is magnified.

Answer: magnified and inverted

questions.q:
Below we give four entries for the truth table of two point input OR gate. Which two are wrong?
$\begin{array}{cccc} & A & B & Y\\ \text{i} & 1 & 0 & 1\\ \text{ii} & 1 & 1 & 0\\ \text{iii} & 0 & 0 & 1\\ \text{iv} & 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}$
questions.solution:
The Boolean expression for an OR gate is $Y = A + B$.

Evaluating each given entry:

For (i): $A = 1, B = 0 \Rightarrow Y = 1 + 0 = 1$. This is correct.

For (ii): $A = 1, B = 1 \Rightarrow Y = 1 + 1 = 1$. The given value is $0$, so this is wrong.

For (iii): $A = 0, B = 0 \Rightarrow Y = 0 + 0 = 0$. The given value is $1$, so this is wrong.

For (iv): $A = 0, B = 1 \Rightarrow Y = 0 + 1 = 1$. This is correct.

The wrong entries are (ii) and (iii).

Answer: (ii) and (iii)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a common emitter amplifier, the audio signal voltage across the collector resistance of $2\ \text{k}\Omega$ is 4 V. If the current amplification factor of the transistor is 100 and the base resistance is $1\ \text{k}\Omega$, then the input voltage is
questions.solution:
Output voltage $V_o = 4\ \text{V}$

Collector resistance $R_c = 2\ \text{k}\Omega = 2000\ \Omega$

Collector current $I_c = \dfrac{V_o}{R_c} = \dfrac{4}{2000} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A}$

Current amplification factor $\beta = 100$

Base current $I_b = \dfrac{I_c}{\beta} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}}{100} = 2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{A}$

Base resistance $R_b = 1\ \text{k}\Omega = 1000\ \Omega$

Input voltage $V_i = I_b R_b = (2 \times 10^{-5}) \times 1000 = 2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{V} = 20\ \text{mV}$

Answer: $20\ \text{mV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following statements is NOT TRUE?
options: The majority carriers in n-type semiconductors are electrons.
The resistance of an intrinsic semiconductor decreases with increase in temperature.
Doping pure silicon crystal with trivalent impurities gives p-type semiconductor.
The majority carriers in n-type semiconductors are holes.
questions.solution:
In an n-type semiconductor, pentavalent impurities are added to the pure semiconductor. Each pentavalent atom donates one electron to the conduction band. Therefore, electrons are the majority charge carriers and holes are the minority charge carriers.

The statement 'The majority carriers in n-type semiconductors are holes' is incorrect.

The resistance of an intrinsic semiconductor decreases with an increase in temperature because more electron-hole pairs are generated, increasing conductivity.

Doping pure silicon with trivalent impurities creates a deficiency of electrons (holes), resulting in a p-type semiconductor.

Answer: The majority carriers in n-type semiconductors are holes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The rectangular surface area $(12\ \text{cm}\times6\ \text{cm})$ of the black body, at a temperature $127^\circ\text{C}$, emits heat energy at the rate of Q units per second. If the length and breadth of the surface area are each reduced to half of its initial value and the temperature is increased to $327^\circ\text{C}$, then the emission of heat energy will be
questions.solution:
According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the rate of heat emission is given by $E = \sigma A T^4$.

Initial area $A_1 = 12 \times 6 = 72\ \text{cm}^2$

Initial temperature $T_1 = 127^\circ\text{C} = 400\ \text{K}$

Initial rate of heat emission $Q_1 = Q$

Final area $A_2 = \dfrac{12}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{2} = 18\ \text{cm}^2 = \dfrac{A_1}{4}$

Final temperature $T_2 = 327^\circ\text{C} = 600\ \text{K}$

Using the relation $Q \propto A T^4$, we get:

$\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1} \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{Q_2}{Q} = \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{600}{400}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{Q_2}{Q} = \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^4 = \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{81}{16} = \dfrac{81}{64}$

$Q_2 = \dfrac{81Q}{64}$

Answer: $\dfrac{81Q}{64}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal sphere cools from $80^\circ\text{C}$ to $60^\circ\text{C}$ in 10 minute. The time taken (in minute) by it to cool from $60^\circ\text{C}$ to $40^\circ\text{C}$ if the room temperature is $30^\circ\text{C}$, is
questions.solution:
Using Newton's law of cooling in approximation form:

$\dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = K \left( \dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0 \right)$

For the first interval:

$\dfrac{80 - 60}{10} = K \left( \dfrac{80 + 60}{2} - 30 \right)$

$2 = K (70 - 30)$

$2 = 40 K \Rightarrow K = \dfrac{1}{20}$

For the second interval:

$\dfrac{60 - 40}{t} = K \left( \dfrac{60 + 40}{2} - 30 \right)$

$\dfrac{20}{t} = K (50 - 30)$

$\dfrac{20}{t} = 20 K$

Substituting the value of $K$:

$\dfrac{20}{t} = 20 \times \dfrac{1}{20}$

$\dfrac{20}{t} = 1$

$t = 20$ minute

Answer: $20$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three spheres P, Q and R, having radii of 2 m, 3 m and 4 m respectively, are coated with lamp-black on their outer surfaces. The wavelengths corresponding to maximum intensity are 200 nm, 300 nm and 400 nm respectively. If the powers radiated by them are $P_P$, $P_Q$ and $P_R$ respectively, then
questions.solution:
Using Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{max} T = b \Rightarrow T = \dfrac{b}{\lambda_{max}}$.

Using Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated by a black body is $P = \sigma A T^4 = \sigma (4\pi r^2) T^4$.

Substituting $T$, we get $P = \sigma (4\pi r^2) \left(\dfrac{b}{\lambda_{max}}\right)^4 \Rightarrow P \propto \dfrac{r^2}{\lambda_{max}^4}$.

For sphere P: $P_P \propto \dfrac{2^2}{(200)^4} \propto \dfrac{4}{16 \times 10^8} \propto \dfrac{1}{4 \times 10^8}$

For sphere Q: $P_Q \propto \dfrac{3^2}{(300)^4} \propto \dfrac{9}{81 \times 10^8} \propto \dfrac{1}{9 \times 10^8}$

For sphere R: $P_R \propto \dfrac{4^2}{(400)^4} \propto \dfrac{16}{256 \times 10^8} \propto \dfrac{1}{16 \times 10^8}$

Comparing the values, $P_P \gt P_Q \gt P_R$.

Thus, $P_P$ is maximum.

Answer: $P_P$ is maximum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A mono-atomic ideal gas, initially at temperature $T_1$ is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston. The gas is allowed to expand adiabatically to a temperature $T_2$ by releasing the piston suddenly. $L_1$ and $L_2$ are the lengths of gas columns before and after the expansion, respectively. The value of $\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}$ is $\left[\gamma=\dfrac{5}{3}\right]$
questions.solution:
For a reversible adiabatic process, the relationship between temperature and volume is given by $TV^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$.

Applying this to the initial and final states of the gas:

$T_1 V_1^{\gamma - 1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma - 1}$

$\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^{\gamma - 1}$

Let $A$ be the cross-sectional area of the cylinder. The volume of the gas column of length $L$ is $V = AL$.

Substituting $V_1 = AL_1$ and $V_2 = AL_2$:

$\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \left(\dfrac{AL_2}{AL_1}\right)^{\gamma - 1} = \left(\dfrac{L_2}{L_1}\right)^{\gamma - 1}$

Given that the gas is mono-atomic, $\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$.

$\gamma - 1 = \dfrac{5}{3} - 1 = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Substituting this value into the equation:

$\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \left(\dfrac{L_2}{L_1}\right)^{\dfrac{2}{3}}$

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{L_2}{L_1}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas for which $\gamma$ is $3/2$ is heated at constant pressure. The percentage of heat supplied for external work is nearly
questions.solution:
Heat supplied at constant pressure is given by $\Delta Q = n C_p \Delta T$

Work done by the gas is given by $\Delta W = P \Delta V = n R \Delta T$

The fraction of heat supplied used for external work is $\dfrac{\Delta W}{\Delta Q} = \dfrac{n R \Delta T}{n C_p \Delta T} = \dfrac{R}{C_p}$

Using Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$ and $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v}$, we get $C_p - \dfrac{C_p}{\gamma} = R$

$\dfrac{R}{C_p} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\gamma}$

Given $\gamma = \dfrac{3}{2}$, substituting this value:

$\dfrac{\Delta W}{\Delta Q} = 1 - \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Percentage of heat used for external work $= \dfrac{1}{3} \times 100\% = 33.33\%$

This is nearly $33\%$.

Answer: $33\ \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In Young's double slit, 18 fringes are observed to be formed in a certain segment of the screen when light of wavelength 400 nm is used. If the wavelength is changed to 600 nm, the number of fringes observed in the same segment of the screen is
questions.solution:
Let the length of the segment on the screen be $y$.

The fringe width is given by $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.

The number of fringes $n$ in the segment $y$ is $n = \dfrac{y}{\beta} = \dfrac{y d}{\lambda D}$.

This implies that $n \lambda = \text{constant}$, or $n_1 \lambda_1 = n_2 \lambda_2$.

Given $n_1 = 18$, $\lambda_1 = 400 \text{ nm}$, and $\lambda_2 = 600 \text{ nm}$.

Substituting the values, we get:

$18 \times 400 = n_2 \times 600$

$n_2 = \dfrac{18 \times 400}{600} = 12$

Thus, 12 fringes will be observed in the same segment.

Answer: $12$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In Young's double slit experiment using a monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$. The path difference (in terms of an integer n) corresponding to any point having one fourth of its peak intensity is
$\{\cos(\pi/3)=1/2,\ \cos(4\pi/3)=-1/2\}$
questions.solution:
The intensity at any point in Young's double slit experiment is given by $I = I_0 \cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$

Given that $I = \dfrac{I_0}{4}$

$\dfrac{I_0}{4} = I_0 \cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$

$\cos\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right) = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\dfrac{\phi}{2} = n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

$\phi = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

The phase difference $\phi$ is related to the path difference $\Delta x$ by $\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$

$\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x = 2\pi\left(n \pm \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

$\Delta x = \left(n \pm \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\lambda$

Answer: $\left(n\pm\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\lambda,\ n=0,1,2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The density of oxygen is 16 times that of hydrogen. The ratio of the velocity of sound in oxygen to that in hydrogen is
questions.solution:
The velocity of sound in a gas is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}}$.

For oxygen and hydrogen, both being diatomic gases, the ratio of specific heats $\gamma$ is the same. Assuming they are at the same pressure $P$, the velocity of sound is inversely proportional to the square root of the density of the gas.

$v \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}}$

$\dfrac{v_{O}}{v_{H}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_{H}}{\rho_{O}}}$

Given $\rho_{O} = 16 \rho_{H}$,

$\dfrac{v_{O}}{v_{H}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_{H}}{16 \rho_{H}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

The ratio of the velocity of sound in oxygen to that in hydrogen is $1:4$.

Answer: $1:4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical straight wires are stretched so as to produce 8 beats per second when vibrating simultaneously with tensions $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. On changing the tensions, the beat frequency remains unchanged. This will happen when $(T_1 \gt T_2)$
options: both $T_1$ and $T_2$ is decreased by value 256 N
both $T_1$ and $T_2$ is increased by value 256 N
questions.solution:
The frequency of a stretched wire is given by $f = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$.

Since $T_1 \gt T_2$, the initial frequencies satisfy $f_1 \gt f_2$.

The initial beat frequency is $f_1 - f_2 = 8$.

For the beat frequency to remain unchanged after changing the tensions, the new frequencies must satisfy $|f_1' - f_2'| = 8$.

If $T_1$ is changed while $T_2$ is kept constant, we need $|f_1' - f_2| = 8$. Since $f_1 - f_2 = 8$, the only other possibility is $f_2 - f_1' = 8 \Rightarrow f_1' = f_2 - 8 = f_1 - 16$. This requires $f_1$ to decrease, meaning $T_1$ must be decreased.

If $T_2$ is changed while $T_1$ is kept constant, we need $|f_1 - f_2'| = 8$. Since $f_1 - f_2 = 8$, the only other possibility is $f_2' - f_1 = 8 \Rightarrow f_2' = f_1 + 8 = f_2 + 16$. This requires $f_2$ to increase, meaning $T_2$ must be increased.

Thus, the beat frequency can remain unchanged if $T_1$ is decreased or $T_2$ is increased.

Answer: $T_1$ is decreased or $T_2$ is increased

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The length of a sonometer wire AB is 176 cm. Where should the two bridges be placed from end A to divide the wire into three segments whose fundamental frequencies are in the ratio $1:2:3$?
questions.solution:
Let the lengths of the three segments be $l_1$, $l_2$, and $l_3$.

The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{2l}$. Since the tension and mass per unit length are constant for the wire, $f \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$.

Given the ratio of fundamental frequencies is $f_1 : f_2 : f_3 = 1 : 2 : 3$.

Therefore, the ratio of their lengths is $l_1 : l_2 : l_3 = 1 : \dfrac{1}{2} : \dfrac{1}{3} = 6 : 3 : 2$.

Let $l_1 = 6x$, $l_2 = 3x$, and $l_3 = 2x$.

The total length of the wire is $l_1 + l_2 + l_3 = 176 \text{ cm}$.

$6x + 3x + 2x = 176 \Rightarrow 11x = 176 \Rightarrow x = 16 \text{ cm}$.

The lengths of the individual segments are:
$l_1 = 6 \times 16 = 96 \text{ cm}$
$l_2 = 3 \times 16 = 48 \text{ cm}$
$l_3 = 2 \times 16 = 32 \text{ cm}$

The positions of the two bridges from end A are $l_1$ and $l_1 + l_2$.

First bridge position $= 96 \text{ cm}$.

Second bridge position $= 96 + 48 = 144 \text{ cm}$.

Answer: 96 cm and 144 cm

questions.q:
A wave is represented by the equation $y=0.2\sin 4\pi\left[\dfrac{t}{0.08}+\dfrac{x}{0.8}+\dfrac{1}{12}\right]$ in SI units.
The expression represents a wave traveling in the
options: positive x-direction with velocity 10 m/s and with wavelength 0.4 m.
negative x-direction with velocity 10 m/s and with wavelength 0.4 m.
positive x-direction with velocity 20 m/s and with wavelength 0.6 m.
negative x-direction with velocity 20 m/s and with wavelength 0.6 m.
questions.solution:
The given wave equation is $y = 0.2 \sin 4\pi \left[ \dfrac{t}{0.08} + \dfrac{x}{0.8} + \dfrac{1}{12} \right]$

Comparing this with the standard wave equation $y = A \sin(\omega t + kx + \phi)$

$\omega = \dfrac{4\pi}{0.08} = 50\pi$ rad/s

$k = \dfrac{4\pi}{0.8} = 5\pi$ rad/m

Since the signs of $\omega t$ and $kx$ are the same, the wave is traveling in the negative x-direction.

The velocity of the wave is $v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{50\pi}{5\pi} = 10$ m/s

The wavelength is $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5\pi} = 0.4$ m

Answer: negative x-direction with velocity 10 m/s and with wavelength 0.4 m.
